bundle.name: Australia and New Zealand: eight days worth cloning
bundle.description: Eight day-shaped playbooks from Sydney's eastern beaches, Melbourne's laneways, Wavelength's outer-reef moorings out of Port Douglas, Uluru, and four New Zealand days - Queenstown at full blowout, Milford Sound from Te Anau, the Tongariro Alpine Crossing, and Hobbiton with Rotorua's thermal ground. Priced at what these two countries honestly cost, with the shuttle rules, road closures, seasonal shutdowns and booking lead times that decide whether the day works at all.
sources: PARTIALLY VERIFIED 2026-09-06: gating facts (opening days, hours, seasonal and weather access rules, shuttle and booking requirements) were checked against the official sources listed below for 8 of 8 days. Prices were NOT systematically verified and remain model estimates - see KI-2026-09-06-d.

playbooks.name: Bondi to Coogee at dawn, Surry Hills after dark
playbooks.summary: The eastern beaches walk done in the only order that works — south from Bondi with the sun behind you, four swims on the way, and the bus back into town for the best dinner in Sydney.

sourceTrip.name: Three weeks down the east coast

stops.title: First swim of the day in the Icebergs pool
stops.notes: Ten dollars at the turnstile, and it buys you the pool before the photographers arrive around nine. Two things to know: the pool closes all day Thursday for cleaning, and on a big south swell the sea breaks straight over the end wall, which is thrilling if you were expecting it and alarming if you were not. Swim laps in the 50 m, then get out — the day is long. Lockers take coins. Verified 2026-09-06: the Thursday cleaning closure is real (the club notes it may open on summer Thursdays when the tides allow), pool hours are 06:00-18:30 Mon-Fri and 06:30-18:30 weekends, and adult entry is A$10 with towel or locker hire A$5 each, so this 06:50 slot is inside opening hours on any day but Thursday.

stops.title: Coffee and a bacon roll on Hall Street
stops.notes: Eat before the walk, not after. There is precisely one good coffee between Bondi and Coogee — the Bronte kiosks — and it always has a queue twelve deep by nine. Two blocks back from the sand on Hall Street the prices drop by a third and the seats exist. Fill a water bottle here too; the bubblers along the path work but they are warm.

stops.title: Walk south: Bondi to Tamarama to Bronte, swim at Bronte Baths

location.name: Bondi to Bronte coastal path via Marks Park

stops.notes: Walk it north to south. The six kilometres are the same either way, but southbound the morning sun is behind you rather than in the lens, the climbs are shorter, and you end at Coogee where the bus back to the city runs every ten minutes instead of at Bondi where it runs full. Mackenzies Bay between Bondi and Tamarama only has sand a few months a year — if it is there, it is a beach that comes and goes. At Bronte swim in the Baths at the south end, not the bogey hole, and do not swim the Bronte Express rip in the middle of the beach. In late October and early November Sculpture by the Sea puts 100,000 people on this path: the same walk at 07:00 is empty and the sculptures are all still there.

stops.title: Waverley Cemetery boardwalk, then snorkel the Clovelly channel
stops.notes: The clifftop boardwalk through Waverley Cemetery is the prettiest 500 metres of the whole route and half the walkers cut inland and miss it — it closes for storm repairs occasionally, and the detour up Trafalgar Street is signposted when it does. Clovelly is the swim to plan around: a narrow concrete-sided inlet, flat when everything else is churning, with resident blue gropers that come to look at you. Hire a mask at the kiosk if you are not carrying one. Go at high tide for depth, and never at the mouth on a big swell — the surge in that channel is stronger than it looks. Gordons Bay, five minutes further, has an underwater nature trail if you have time and your own gear.

stops.title: Wylie's Baths on the ocean rocks
stops.notes: Everyone finishes at Coogee Beach; the finish is actually 400 m past it. Wylie's is a 1907 tidal pool on the rocks, entry about ten dollars, timber deck, and the water has whatever the ocean sent it that morning — seaweed, small fish, sometimes an octopus in the corner. Lower tide means shallower and warmer. The women-only McIvers Baths next door is the other one, cash donation at the gate.

stops.title: Late lunch upstairs at the Coogee Pavilion
stops.notes: Ground floor is families and ping-pong; the rooftop is 18+ and has the view. No bookings for small groups on the roof, so arrive before one on a weekend or you will wait 40 minutes. If it is heaving, A Fish Called Coogee does fish and chips two minutes away and you eat them on the grass.

stops.title: Bus 373 back to town, shower, change

location.name: Coogee Beach bus interchange, Arden Street

stops.notes: Tap on with a credit card or phone — no Opal card needed, and the daily cap applies to contactless the same way. The 373 runs Coogee to the CBD; the X73 is the express in peak. Do not try to do this walk and then drive: parking at both ends is metered, patrolled and full by nine.

stops.title: Dinner at Firedoor, everything over wood
stops.notes: No gas, no electricity in the kitchen — every plate comes off wood, and the fish is dry-aged for days before it gets near a fire. Bookings open about two months ahead and the counter seats facing the fire are released at the same time; take those over a table. If you cannot get in, Porteno two streets over does whole animals on the asado from midday and keeps a walk-in bar, and the Dolphin Hotel's wine room takes walk-ins until late. Budget for the chef's menu with a glass — this is the day's one big spend.

playbooks.name: Melbourne laneways: a coffee crawl with an art gallery attached
playbooks.summary: A weekday walked at coffee pace — standing room at Patricia, borek in the Queen Vic deli hall, the Great Hall ceiling on your back, and dinner at the bar at Cumulus.

stops.title: Stand up and drink it at Patricia

location.name: Patricia Coffee Brewers, cnr Little Bourke and Little William

stops.notes: There are no seats. That is the whole design — you stand at the shelf, drink it, and leave, which is why the queue moves even when it is out the door at 08:15. Weekdays only: Patricia is shut Saturday and Sunday, and a laneway coffee day planned for a weekend has to start at Market Lane instead. The magic in a glass is what to order; the white chocolate mendiant comes with it.

stops.title: Second breakfast in the Queen Vic deli hall
stops.notes: Check the day before you plan around this: the market is closed Mondays and Wednesdays, which catches out more visitors than any other rule in this city. Go to the Deli Hall (the enclosed one), get a borek from the Turkish counter and a bratwurst if it is cold, then a filter at Market Lane's Therry Street shop on the way out. Fruit and veg sheds discount hard in the last hour, not the first. Verified 2026-09-06: Queen Victoria Market is closed all day Monday and Wednesday (the Wednesday night market, 17:00-22:00, runs only in season), and trades Tue/Thu/Fri 06:00-15:00, Sat 06:00-16:00, Sun 09:00-16:00. This 08:25 stop therefore only works Tuesday, Thursday, Friday or Saturday - on a Sunday the market is still shut at 08:25, and on Monday or Wednesday the day needs a different second breakfast.

stops.title: Hosier Lane, Centre Place, Degraves, Presgrave

location.name: Hosier Lane and the Flinders Lane arcades

stops.notes: Hosier Lane before 10:30 or not at all — the walking tours land on the half hour and the lane is 3 m wide. The walls are repainted constantly, so nothing you saw in a photo is still there; that is the point rather than a disappointment. Then cut through Centre Place and Degraves for the cafe-table version, and find Presgrave Place off Howey Place, which is the one nobody photographs: a lane hung with framed miniatures and tiny installations. Cathedral Arcade in the Nicholas Building has the leadlight dome worth a lift ride.

stops.title: NGV International and the Great Hall ceiling
stops.notes: The permanent collection is free, always — you only pay for the summer blockbuster, and those sell timed slots that go weeks ahead. Walk through the water wall, go straight to the Great Hall and lie down on the carpet: the Leonard French stained-glass ceiling is meant to be seen flat on your back and the guards will not mind. Ninety minutes is enough for one wing; trying to do the whole building is how this day dies. Verified 2026-09-06: NGV International is open daily 10:00-17:00 and entry to the permanent collection is free, so a 10:40 arrival is fine and the building closes well before this day needs it to.

stops.title: Lunch at the bar at Supernormal
stops.notes: Lunch is the way into the Flinders Lane restaurants you cannot book for dinner. Supernormal keeps bar seats for walk-ins and turns them fast; the lobster roll is the thing people queue for and it is worth it once. Chin Chin two doors down runs the same walk-in-and-wait system and sends you to the basement bar while you wait, which is a decent place to be waiting.

stops.title: Tram 86 to Collingwood for Proud Mary
stops.notes: The Free Tram Zone stops at the edge of the CBD — the moment you cross into Collingwood you need a Myki, and the daily cap is a few dollars, so buy the card and stop thinking about it. Proud Mary roasts its own and is the reason half of Melbourne's other cafes taste the way they do. Weekend brunch there is a 45-minute wait; a Tuesday at two, you walk in. Walk back down Smith Street rather than taking the tram — it is 20 minutes of the best browsing in the city.

stops.title: A negroni standing up at Bar Americano
stops.notes: A tiled room the size of a bathroom that fits about ten people standing, hidden in the lane you found this morning. Cash used to be the rule and the no-photos house style still is. The drinks are expensive and correct. If it is full — it is often full by six — Siglo's terrace above the Supper Club has the Parliament view and a fireplace.

stops.title: Dinner at Cumulus Inc
stops.notes: Book the table, but know that the long marble bar is walk-in only and is the better seat — you watch the pass and you never wait for service. Order the tuna tartare, the madeleines, and something from the rotisserie to share. It runs from breakfast to late, so a 21:00 table is a real option if the earlier sittings are gone.

playbooks.name: Port Douglas: the outer reef on a small boat
playbooks.summary: Past the inner reef to Wavelength's own outer-reef moorings with a marine biologist and a small boat, not a pontoon with 400 - and back in time for a beer on Macrossan Street.

sourceTrip.name: Queensland: reef, rainforest, and a lot of driving

stops.title: Breakfast early, and take the tablet now
stops.notes: Seasickness medication works taken an hour before boarding and does almost nothing taken on the boat when you already feel it — this is the single highest-value line in this day. Eat something plain and eat it now: the crossing is 90 minutes and the trade winds pick up from about May to October, when 20-25 knot forecasts make it a genuinely bouncy ride out. Check the Bureau's coastal waters forecast for Cairns the night before rather than trusting the tour desk.

stops.title: Check in at the Crystalbrook Superyacht Marina
stops.notes: Check-in is 30 minutes before departure and the boats leave on the hour they say they leave — Wavelength at 08:30, Poseidon at 08:30, Quicksilver's pontoon run later at 10:00. The marina car park is free and fills; a 12-minute walk from anywhere in town beats circling. Reef-safe sunscreen only, and a rash vest saves more skin than any bottle. Verified 2026-09-06: boarding for Wavelength is from 08:10 at the Crystalbrook Superyacht Marina (the marina formerly branded Marina Mirage) and the boat is back in Port Douglas about 16:00; the Wavelength shop itself is in the Reef Marina building, not at the berth, so go to the boat.

stops.title: Crossing to Wavelength's outer-reef moorings
stops.notes: CORRECTED 2026-09-06: this day was written as Wavelength going to the Agincourt ribbon reefs, and it does not. Wavelength's own site says it holds exclusive outer-reef moorings on Opal Reef, St Crispin Reef and Tongue Reef and picks three of them on the day, and it markets those sites as seeing far fewer visitors than the Agincourt Reefs. Agincourt is where Quicksilver's pontoon goes. So: same continental-shelf edge, same 90-minute crossing, different reefs - and if you specifically want Agincourt you are booking Quicksilver, not this. Wavelength is snorkel-only (no divers to wait for) and caps the boat at 58 guests on a vessel built for 100, not the 30 this day used to claim. The price includes the reef environmental management charge and the daily park fee; check that when comparing quotes, because some operators quote before it. If the forecast is over 25 knots, the honest alternative is Quicksilver's pontoon: a much larger crowd but a fixed platform that does not move.

stops.title: First site: guided snorkel with the marine biologist

location.name: Wavelength site one, Opal or Tongue Reef

stops.notes: Take the guided snorkel on the first site even if you are a confident swimmer — you spend an hour being shown what you would otherwise swim over, and the guides are reef researchers who log what they see. From November to May you wear a full lycra stinger suit: irukandji and box jellyfish are the reason, they are not optional, and hire is a few dollars. Also: a stinger suit is a sun suit, which matters more than people expect at 16 degrees south. Verified 2026-09-06: marine biologists guide a snorkel and give a reef talk every day the boat runs, and stinger season is early November to late May. The suits are not optional on the boat and are included in the fare; note that the serious box jellyfish and irukandji risk is inshore, on beaches and estuaries, and is considerably lower out at the shelf edge - the suit out here is as much a sun suit as anything.

stops.title: Second site, then lunch on the back deck

location.name: Wavelength site two, Opal or St Crispin Reef

stops.notes: The crew move the boat to a second and third site rather than parking all day, and each site is a different structure — a bommie field, then a wall. Lunch is included and served on the crossing between sites. Eat lightly, get back in the water within 20 minutes, and skip the third site only if you are cold; the water is 24-29 degrees depending on the month and an hour still gets you.

stops.title: Third site, then the run home
stops.notes: The run home is usually downwind and faster than the run out. Sit outside and at the back if your stomach is uncertain, and look for the low outline of the Low Isles on the port side. Boats are alongside about 16:30, which leaves the whole evening — do not book anything before 17:30 in case the swell adds half an hour. Verified 2026-09-06: Wavelength quotes a return to Port Douglas of approximately 16:00, not 16:30, so this window has been pulled back an hour earlier at the end. Still do not book anything before 17:30 in case the swell adds half an hour.

stops.title: Sunset on Four Mile Beach
stops.notes: Walk it, do not swim it in stinger season unless you are inside the netted enclosure at the southern end — and the net stops jellyfish, not crocodiles, which is why nobody swims at dawn or dusk near the creek mouths here. Flagstaff Hill is a 25-minute climb from the far end for the view back over the bay if your legs still work.

stops.title: Dinner at Salsa Bar and Grill

location.name: Salsa Bar and Grill, Wharf Street

stops.notes: Book it in the morning before you get on the boat — you will have no phone signal at the reef and Salsa is full by seven every night in the dry season. Coral trout or barramundi, and the wine list is better than a beach town has any right to. Hemingway's brewery at the marina is the walk-in fallback and the beer is made 200 m from the table.

playbooks.name: Uluru: sunrise at Talinguru, the base walk, and the desert lit up
playbooks.summary: The rock from every side on foot before the heat, an afternoon that respects it, and a night that ends among 50,000 stems of light.

sourceTrip.name: Red Centre, three nights at Yulara

stops.title: Out of Yulara in the dark

location.name: Yulara to the park entry station

stops.notes: The park gates open before sunrise and the opening time moves every month — it is roughly half an hour before first light, so check the month's hours rather than assuming. Yulara to the Talinguru car park is about 25 minutes. Have the pass on your phone before you leave: there is no reliable signal at the gate. Cost here is a day of a small hire car plus fuel out of Yulara, which is the most expensive fuel you will buy in Australia — fill up before you leave Alice if you drove. Verified 2026-09-06: park gate hours move with the sun across the year - roughly 05:00 to 21:00 in December and January, narrowing to about 06:30 to 19:30 in June and July. This 04:50 departure is a December-to-February plan. In June or July the gate is still shut at 05:20 and sunrise is not until about 07:20, so the whole morning shifts about ninety minutes later and the base walk starts nearer 09:00. Check the month's posted hours before you set an alarm.

stops.title: Sunrise from Talinguru Nyakunytjaku
stops.notes: Talinguru is the sunrise side, and the reason to use it rather than any other pull-off is that from the top of the dune boardwalk you can see Uluru and Kata Tjuta in the same frame as the light arrives. Get there 40 minutes before sunrise: the near car park fills first and the walk from the far one is ten minutes in the dark, so carry a head torch. The park pass is a three-day ticket bought online, roughly 38 dollars, and it is checked. Do not go to the sunset viewing area at dawn — you will be looking into a shadow. Verified 2026-09-06: the three-day park pass is A$38 per adult and under-18s are free; buy it online and have it on the phone, because it is scanned at the entry station.

stops.title: The full base walk, anticlockwise from Mala

location.name: Uluru base walk, Mala car park trailhead

stops.notes: 10.6 km, flat, three hours at a walking pace, and it is the thing to do here — the rock is not one shape, it is a dozen, and you only learn that by walking around it. Start at Mala and go anticlockwise so the sun stays off your face longest. Climbing has been closed permanently since October 2019 at the request of the Anangu traditional owners; the old chain route is still visible and is not a path. Several sites — Mala and the Kuniya side near Mutitjulu waterhole — are signposted no-photography for cultural reasons, and rangers do ask. Carry three litres per person minimum, refill at the Mala and Kuniya tanks, and take the free Mala ranger walk at 08:00 in the cooler months if you would rather be told the stories than read them. When the forecast tops 36 the walks close from 11:00, which is another argument for starting at seven.

stops.title: Dot-painting workshop with Maruku Arts at the Cultural Centre
stops.notes: Ninety minutes with an Anangu artist and an interpreter, learning the iconography before you paint anything — it is the best-value cultural hour in the park and about 89 dollars. Book the day before; morning sessions run daily and sell out in peak season. The Cultural Centre itself is free, has no photography inside, and Maruku's shop is where you buy work directly from the artists rather than from a gallery in Alice. Verified 2026-09-06: the Cultural Centre is open 07:00-17:45 daily, so this 10:30-12:15 workshop sits comfortably inside its hours.

stops.title: Lunch and lie down at the resort in the worst of the heat
stops.notes: Plan the middle of the day as nothing. Between 12:00 and 15:00 from October to March the desert is genuinely dangerous to walk in and the shade at the resort is where everyone sensible is. Kulata is staffed by Anangu hospitality trainees and is the cheapest decent food in Yulara; the IGA in Town Square is cheaper still if you want to build a lunch. There is a free guided garden walk and a bush yarn session at Town Square most afternoons.

stops.title: Fifteen minutes over the rock by helicopter
stops.notes: The 15-minute Uluru flight is about 185 dollars and it does one thing the ground cannot: it shows you that Kata Tjuta is bigger than Uluru and 30 km away, which no photograph from the base ever conveys. If the budget stretches, the 25-30 minute flight adds Kata Tjuta properly. Afternoon flights fly into better light than morning ones. Skip it entirely if it is windy — they cancel and refund rather than fly rough, so keep it late enough in the day that a cancellation does not wreck anything.

stops.title: Sounds of Silence dinner under the stars

location.name: Sounds of Silence dune-top dining area

stops.notes: Canapes and sparkling on a dune with Uluru on one side and Kata Tjuta on the other while the sun goes, then a bush-tucker buffet at shared tables, then all the lights go out and someone talks you through the Southern Cross and the Emu in the Sky. About 295 dollars, includes transfers from every hotel in the resort, and it books out weeks ahead in the cool season. The smaller, seated, four-course Tali Wiru is the upgrade and only runs roughly April to October. Take a jacket: winter nights here drop near freezing after a 22-degree day. Verified 2026-09-06: Sounds of Silence is a four-hour experience door to door including the hotel transfer, not the three and a quarter this day allowed, so the window now runs to 21:45. The start moves with sunset - earlier in winter, well after 19:00 in midsummer - so take the pick-up time you are given rather than this one.

stops.title: Field of Light, as part of the dinner package

location.name: Field of Light, Bruce Munro installation

stops.notes: CORRECTED 2026-09-06: this was written as a separate Star Pass session stacked after dinner, and that does not fit. Sounds of Silence is a four-hour evening ending with your transfer back to the hotel, and Field of Light general admission is itself about 90 minutes, so the two only work as one booking. Ayers Rock Resort sells exactly that: a combined Field of Light + Sounds of Silence dinner, where the 50,000 solar stems come on as darkness falls beside the dining dune and you walk down into the field as the night ends, with one transfer instead of two. Book that combination rather than the dinner and a standalone Star Pass, and treat this window as the tail of the same evening, not a second outing. If you would rather do the field on its own, do it on a different night - the last session, when the earlier groups have cleared. Phone cameras make a mess of it; look instead.

playbooks.name: Queenstown, no restraint: 134 metres, 15,000 feet, and a tasting menu
playbooks.summary: The blowout day this town exists to sell — the Nevis, a skydive over the Wakatipu basin, a snow landing in the Remarkables, and Amisfield to put you back together.

sourceTrip.name: South Island, two weeks, one very expensive Tuesday

stops.title: Breakfast at Vudu, and do not overdo it

location.name: Vudu Cafe and Larder, Beach Street

stops.notes: Eat something, but eat small — you have a bungy at nine and a skydive at two. The lakefront Vudu on Beach Street has the view; the original on Rees Street has the shorter queue. Both are cash-flow-positive on flat whites by 08:30, so order at the counter and take a table outside.

stops.title: Nevis shuttle from The Station

location.name: The Station, cnr Camp and Shotover Streets

stops.notes: You cannot drive yourself to the Nevis — it is 40 minutes up a private 4WD farm track and the transfer is part of the ticket, leaving from The Station in town. Check in 30 minutes before your slot. Weigh-in happens here and the number goes on your hand in marker, which is how they set the cord; there is a minimum and a maximum weight and it is not negotiable. Verified 2026-09-06: the Bungy Bus leaves from the AJ Hackett Queenstown Bungy Centre on the corner of Camp and Shotover Streets, the first departure of the day is 08:40 and they run every 40 minutes to 14:40, and check-in is 30 minutes before your bus. The old 08:15 departure in this day was not a real bus time - this window is now check-in for the 08:40.

stops.title: The Nevis Bungy: 134 metres, 8.5 seconds
stops.notes: New Zealand's highest, from a pod slung on cables over the canyon — around 305 dollars, and the trip out and back is about three and a half hours all in. Two pieces of advice from people who have done all three local jumps: the Nevis is the one where the walk out along the cable to the pod is worse than the jump, and going first in your group is much easier than going eighth. The Kawarau bridge jump is half the price, a third of the height, and the one to pick if you only want to say you did it. Wind stops the Nevis more often than rain; they rebook the same day when they can. Verified 2026-09-06: AJ Hackett tells you to allow four hours total from the Bungy Centre, so the 08:40 bus has you back in town about 12:40 rather than 12:15; the freefall is 8.5 seconds off 134 metres as described.

stops.title: Fergburger, eaten on a wall
stops.notes: The queue looks worse than it is — it moves, and they text you when it is ready, so join it, walk away, and come back. Order at the window, then get Fergbaker next door to hold a pie for later. If the line is genuinely round the corner, Devil Burger does the same job in ten minutes.

stops.title: Skydive over the Wakatipu basin from 15,000 feet
stops.notes: Fifteen thousand feet is about 60 seconds of freefall and roughly 479 dollars; the 12,000 ft option is cheaper for 45 seconds and honestly the difference is not the money. Book the earliest slot you can and expect to be moved: cloud base decides everything, and they roll jumps down the day rather than cancel them, which is exactly why this sits before dinner and not after. The photo package is a hard sell at the hangar — decide before you go up, not while you are buzzing.

stops.title: Snow landing high in the Remarkables

location.name: Glacier Southern Lakes Helicopters, Lucas Place

stops.notes: A 30-minute alpine flight with a landing on the snow, around 495 dollars, and the landing is the whole point: you stand on a ridge in absolute silence with the Wakatipu 1,500 m below. Hold it rather than book it — alpine landings are the first thing cancelled for wind or low cloud, and the operators will tell you honestly at midday whether the afternoon is flying. If it is a no, the same money buys a Milford Sound fly-cruise-fly on a different day, which is a better use of it than a scenic circuit in flat light.

stops.title: Onsen Hot Pools with the roof open
stops.notes: Private cedar tubs above the Shotover canyon, booked by the pool rather than the person, with a roof and a wall that retract — book the last light slot and ask for a west-facing room. It is 15 minutes out of town and they run a free shuttle if you ask when booking. After a bungy and a skydive this is not a luxury, it is maintenance.

stops.title: Trust the chef at Amisfield
stops.notes: No menu — you say what you do not eat and they cook, roughly 180 dollars a head with the wine pairing on top, and the pairing is worth taking because the estate pours its own pinot and riesling next to the food they were made for. Book six to eight weeks ahead for dinner; the lunch sitting is far easier to get and arguably better, since you can see the vines and the lake. It is 20 minutes from town on the Arrowtown road, so one of you is not drinking or you have already booked the taxi — Queenstown taxis after 22:00 on a Saturday are a genuine problem.

playbooks.name: Milford Sound the right way: from Te Anau, on the first boat
playbooks.summary: The 119 km road is the trip, not the transfer - leave Te Anau at seven, take the 11:10 small-boat sailing (there is no 10:45), and drive back down the valley with the light behind you.

stops.title: Breakfast in Te Anau and the last fuel there is
stops.notes: Fill the tank in Te Anau. There is no fuel anywhere on the Milford Road — 119 km in, 119 km back, and the only pump at the far end is for boats. Before you turn the key, check the road status: the Milford Road is closed by avalanche risk and slips more often than any other state highway in the country, sometimes for a day, and between June and November you are legally required to carry snow chains in the vehicle even when the sun is out. Rental companies hand them over on request. Buy lunch supplies here too, and sandfly repellent, which is not a joke in Fiordland. Verified 2026-09-06: NZTA and DOC put the legal chain-carrying requirement between Te Anau and Milford at June to November inclusive, not May - the old May date here was wrong - and not carrying them is a fine of up to $750 with roadside checks that turn vehicles back. The avalanche control programme runs the winter season and the road is genuinely closed on average about eight days a year; check the status on the NZTA journey planner or 0800 44 44 49 before you turn the key.

stops.title: SH94 north: Eglinton flats, Mirror Lakes, Monkey Creek
stops.notes: Two hours without stopping, and you will stop, so give it two and a quarter. In order: the Eglinton flats where the beech forest opens out, Mirror Lakes (a five-minute boardwalk, only mirrors on a still morning, which is another argument for going early rather than at midday), Knobs Flat toilets, Pop's View, and Monkey Creek where you can drink straight from the stream and the kea will strip the rubber off your windscreen wipers while you do. Do not feed them. The road is single lane in places with no barrier, and the coaches from Queenstown come the other way from about 09:30 — being ahead of them is the entire trick of this day. Verified 2026-09-06: the stretch between the Hollyford Road junction and The Chasm is a signposted Restricted No Stopping Zone because it is avalanche path - the roadside stops on this list are all south of it, so keep driving through that section rather than pulling over for a photo.

stops.title: Homer Tunnel and the walk into The Chasm

location.name: Homer Tunnel east portal and The Chasm walk

stops.notes: The Homer Tunnel is one lane, unlit, rough-hewn, and runs on traffic lights from October to April with waits up to 15 or 20 minutes — build that in. It drops 10 percent through the mountain and pops you into the Cleddau Valley. The Chasm is a 20-minute return loop over two bridges above water that has drilled the rock into holes; it is the best short walk on the road and nearly everyone on a coach misses it because the coach does not stop. Verified 2026-09-06: the Homer Tunnel traffic lights run over the summer peak with delays of up to about 20 minutes, so keep that in this window.

stops.title: Park and check in at the terminal
stops.notes: Parking at the terminal is paid and enforced, the machine wants a card, and there is no phone signal to fix it if the machine dislikes you, so keep a card that works. It is a ten-minute walk from the car park to the wharf along the foreshore. Check in 20 minutes before departure — boats leave on time and there is no second one for an hour. Verified 2026-09-06: the terminal car park is NZ$10 an hour after the first 20 minutes free (NZ$5 an hour if you arrive after 15:00), the machine wants a card and there is no signal to argue with it; free parking exists at Deepwater Basin Road about 1.5 km back. In high season the main car park is full by about 09:00, which is another reason to be early even for a later sailing.

stops.title: The 11:10 sailing on a small boat
stops.notes: CORRECTED 2026-09-06: there is no 10:45 Mitre Peak Cruises sailing and this day could not be walked as written. Mitre Peak's published departures are 08:50, 09:55, 11:10, 13:30 and 15:55, subject to season, so the 11:10 is the one this drive actually makes - leaving Te Anau at 07:05 does not get you to the terminal in time to check in for the 09:55. Everything about the boat itself checks out: Mitre Peak runs two-hour cruises on purpose-built vessels capped at 75 passengers, gets closer to the walls than the 400-seat ships, and is still operating in 2026; RealNZ and Southern Discoveries run the big boats and the underwater observatory add-on. Hold rather than book if you can, because this is weather-dependent in a specific way: rain is good here - a wet day puts hundreds of temporary waterfalls down the walls - and what ruins it is a storm that cancels sailings outright. The 11:10 is inside the coach crush; the 08:50 or the 15:55 are markedly emptier if you can shift the shape of the day. Sit outside on the bow going out, inside coming back, and expect the boat to nose right under Stirling Falls.

stops.title: Lunch at Pio Pio, up the road from the terminal

location.name: Pio Pio Cafe, Milford Sound Lodge

stops.notes: The terminal cafe is a sandwich in a fridge; Pio Pio at the lodge, a few minutes back down the road, is a proper kitchen with a deck over the river and is the only real food in Milford. It closes in the deep off-season, so check. If you brought lunch from Te Anau instead, eat it at Deepwater Basin rather than the car park — same water, no buses.

stops.title: Back down the valley in the afternoon light

location.name: Milford Road southbound, Hollyford turnoff to Te Anau

stops.notes: Southbound in the afternoon is the good direction — the sun is on the Darran Mountains behind you and the coaches have all gone. Two worthwhile stops if the legs allow: the Lake Marian falls boardwalk off the Hollyford Road (20 minutes return; the full lake is four hours and not today), and Mirror Lakes again, which is a different place with the light from the other side. Watch for keas on the road at the tunnel and for one-lane bridges the whole way.

stops.title: Dinner at Redcliff, and book it this morning
stops.notes: An old settler's cottage that cooks blue cod and Fiordland venison properly and has live music in the back bar most nights in summer — it is the best table in Te Anau by a distance and it has maybe fifteen of them. Ring before you drive out in the morning, because there is no signal in the valley to ring from later. Closed in winter some years, so check the season.

playbooks.name: Tongariro Alpine Crossing: 19.4 km, one direction, no car
playbooks.summary: A one-way alpine traverse with a four-hour parking limit at one end, a DOC track booking your shuttle operator needs you to hold, and a June-to-October winter season when the ordinary shuttles stop running altogether.

stops.title: Eat in the dark and pack for four seasons
stops.notes: Check the mountain forecast, not the town forecast — MetService publishes a Tongariro National Park page and the shuttle operators cancel off it. The crossing tops out at 1,886 m on an exposed ridge with no shelter and no water for 19.4 km; the difference between a fine day and a dangerous one is a wind speed number. Pack three litres of water, a windproof and a warm layer regardless of the temperature at the road, sunscreen, and food for six hours. There are toilets at the trailheads and two composting toilets on the track, and no rubbish bins anywhere. Verified 2026-09-06: DOC's transport concessionaires are required to follow NIWA hazardous weather alerts and one operator had its concession suspended for two weeks in March 2026 for carrying more than 100 walkers through a Hazardous Weather Warning - so if your shuttle cancels, that is the system working, not the operator being timid.

stops.title: Shuttle to Mangatepopo
stops.notes: SEASON WARNING, checked 2026-09-06: from June to October this day does not exist in the form written here. DOC and the crossing's own operators state that the usual shuttle services do not run in winter and the Ketetahi car park is closed for the winter season, reopening 24 October; in winter the crossing is an alpine trip needing helmet, crampons and ice axe with the competence to use them, and the way through is a guided trip booked out of National Park Village, not a shuttle. In season the rule is as described: the crossing is a one-way walk between two car parks 40 minutes' drive apart, and a four-hour parking limit is enforced at the road ends over the October-to-May peak, so you cannot leave a car at either end and walk. Around 45 to 60 dollars from National Park Village, Turangi or Whakapapa, with a fixed Ketetahi pick-up you must make. Verified 2026-09-06 and new since this day was written: DOC now runs a Tongariro Alpine Crossing booking system, and while walkers are not penalised for turning up without one and there is no cap, a track booking IS required to use a shuttle or a guided walk - concessionaires must confirm you hold one, and can make it for you. Sort it when you book the shuttle. Book the earliest departure: you want to be over Red Crater before the afternoon cloud.

stops.title: Mangatepopo Valley to Soda Springs
stops.notes: An hour and a bit of boardwalk and old lava flow, almost flat, and it is the warm-up you should walk slowly — everyone who sprints this section pays for it on the staircase. The Soda Springs side trip is ten minutes return to a waterfall off Mount Ngauruhoe's flank. The last toilet before the climb is here; use it.

stops.title: The Devil's Staircase to South Crater
stops.notes: The hard 200 vertical metres of the day, done first, which is the mercy of walking this direction. Then South Crater opens out flat and unreal, a gravel plain you cross in 20 minutes. Ngauruhoe is on your right; the summit scramble is closed and discouraged out of respect to Ngati Hikairo ki Tongariro and because the scree has killed people. Do not do it.

stops.title: Red Crater ridge, the high point
stops.notes: The ridge to the top is loose, narrow and the one place the wind funnels hard enough to knock people over — this is where a poor forecast turns from unpleasant to genuinely serious. Verified 2026-09-06: from June to October the whole route is an alpine mountaineering trip - DOC lists helmet, crampons and ice axe as essential, with the competence to use them, plus avalanche awareness - and the ordinary shuttles simply stop running for the season, so the only way across is a guided trip. In summer it is just a steep, scenic slog. The descent off the top is loose scree: heels first, small steps, and let the person below get clear before you start.

stops.title: Emerald Lakes and Blue Lake
stops.notes: Lunch spot, and the picture everyone came for — the colour is dissolved minerals from the thermal vents, and the smell is sulphur. Both these lakes are tapu: do not touch or enter the water, and do not eat sitting at the edge of Blue Lake. Walk 20 m back and eat there instead. This is a request from the iwi that the signs make plainly, and it costs you nothing to honour.

stops.title: The long descent to Ketetahi
stops.notes: Nearly three hours and 1,100 m down, first on open switchbacks with Lake Rotoaira and Taupo laid out in front of you, then into bush for the last hour that goes on longer than anyone expects and is where knees fail. Poles earn their keep here. The hot springs you pass are on private Maori land and are closed to the public — the signs mean it. Aim to be at the car park 20 minutes before your shuttle slot, and if you are running late, phone from the bush edge where signal returns.

stops.title: Beer and a burger at Schnapps
stops.notes: Where the shuttle drops everyone and the only place in the village guaranteed to be serving food at half past three. Sit outside if Ruapehu is out. If the crossing was cancelled for weather — which happens often enough that you should hold a spare day — the Taranaki Falls loop from Whakapapa is two flat hours in the same park and stays open in almost anything. Verified 2026-09-06: if you are reading this between June and 24 October, the Ketetahi car park is shut and the shuttle-based version of this day is off - the Taranaki Falls loop from Whakapapa is the fallback and stays open in almost anything.

playbooks.name: Hobbiton first, then the ground that steams
playbooks.summary: Out to Matamata for the early tour before the buses, back to Rotorua for Champagne Pool and the redwoods, and a hangi that is cooked in the ground you have been walking on.

sourceTrip.name: North Island loop with the kids

stops.title: Breakfast at Okere Falls Store
stops.notes: Twenty minutes out of town on the Tauranga road and worth the detour if you are heading north anyway — a general store with a garden bar, a serious beer list for later in the day, and the Kaituna river rapids five minutes' walk away. In town, Ciabatta Bakery opens earlier and does the pastry version of this.

stops.title: Drive to Matamata, straight to the Shire's Rest
stops.notes: Drive to the farm, not to the town. Tours depart from the Shire's Rest on Buckland Road, about 10 minutes outside Matamata; the i-SITE in town is only a pick-up point for people without a car and sending yourself there costs you 20 minutes. Cost here is the day's fuel out of Rotorua and back. Roads are rural and the fog sits in these valleys until nine in winter. Verified 2026-09-06: tours do depart from the Shire's Rest, 501 Buckland Road, Hinuera - but it is about a 20-minute drive from Matamata township, not 10, so leave the margin. Shire's Rest departures run every 30 minutes from 09:30 to 16:00; the Matamata i-SITE version leaves every 45 minutes from 09:30 to 15:30 and is a four-hour trip because it includes the coach both ways.

stops.title: The Hobbiton tour, and a pint at the Green Dragon
stops.notes: Around NZ$130, two and a half hours, guided the whole way — you cannot wander it alone. Departures run every 30 minutes from 09:30 to 16:00 and summer sells out a fortnight ahead, so book, and book an early slot: the set faces the morning sun and the 10:00 group is a third the size of the 13:00. There are no toilets on the set itself for the two hours. It rains here and the tour does not stop for it, so take a jacket rather than an umbrella. The drink at the Green Dragon at the end is included — the ginger beer is the one to get if you are driving, and the Evening Banquet Tour is the upgrade if you would rather eat there than in Rotorua. Verified 2026-09-06: the Signature Tour from the Shire's Rest is 2.5 hours, not 2 - this window has been extended and the rest of the afternoon pushed back accordingly - and the adult fare was NZ$130 as at 25 August 2026. A bus takes you from the Shire's Rest car park onto the set; no cars go in. Advance booking is strongly recommended, particularly in school holidays, weekends and the summer peak.

stops.title: Lunch at the Shire's Rest
stops.notes: Perfectly decent farm cafe food at the departure building, which saves driving into Matamata hungry. If you would rather eat in town, the Redoubt Bar and Eatery on Broadway is the local choice and is ten minutes away.

stops.title: Back to the thermal belt
stops.notes: An hour back, and the smell tells you when you have arrived — hydrogen sulphide, everywhere, and you stop noticing it by dinner. Wai-O-Tapu is a further 25 minutes south of the city on SH5, so do not drive into town first and then back out; go straight past the turnoff.

stops.title: Wai-O-Tapu: Champagne Pool and the Artist's Palette
stops.notes: About 40 dollars for a 3 km loop of boardwalks over ground that is orange, green and violently green. Skip the Lady Knox Geyser: it goes off at 10:15 every morning because a ranger drops soap into it, it does not fit a Hobbiton morning, and it is the least interesting thing here. Stay on the boardwalks — the crust is thin and people have gone through it. Champagne Pool steams hardest on a cold afternoon, which makes winter the better season for photographs. Te Puia in town is the alternative if you want the Pohutu geyser and a Maori cultural centre in one ticket. Verified 2026-09-06: Wai-O-Tapu is open seven days 08:30-16:30 with LAST ADMISSION AT 15:00, closed only on Christmas Day, and the Lady Knox soaping is 10:15 daily as described. That last-admission time is what forces the shape of this afternoon: with a 2.5-hour Hobbiton tour you arrive here about 14:45 and have fifteen minutes of slack. Miss 15:00 and the day's second half is gone.

stops.title: Redwoods Treewalk at dusk
stops.notes: Suspension bridges strung between 117-year-old Californian redwoods, 20 m up. The nightlights version with David Trubridge's lanterns is the one to buy and it starts at dusk, which in a Rotorua winter is barely five o'clock — check the day's start time when you buy, because in midsummer it is not dark until nine and the day ticket is the better deal then. The forest floor walking tracks underneath are free and excellent if you would rather not pay. Verified 2026-09-06: the Treewalk opens daily at 09:00 and closes about 21:00 in winter and midnight in midsummer, and Nightlights starts 20 minutes after sunset - which in September is around 18:20, i.e. after the Te Pa Tu pick-up. Take the day walk here and the hangi in the evening, or move Nightlights to another night. From 1 September 2026 booking a specific date and time for Nightlights is strongly recommended.

stops.title: Hangi and a powhiri at Te Pa Tu
stops.notes: Around 180 dollars for a four-hour evening in the forest: a powhiri welcome, performance, and a hangi lifted out of the earth oven in front of you. They collect from Rotorua hotels around 17:45 to 18:15 depending where you are staying, so the pick-up, not the start time, is what you plan around — confirm yours when you book. Go in with some manners about it: it is a welcome onto a marae-style space, they will ask your group to nominate a chief, and taking that seriously makes the night. Book at least a few days out in summer.
